How to Use This Book
This volume is designed for continuous study. Complete each lesson in order, run every command in a safe
Linux lab, finish the exercises, and mark the unit Completed only when you can explain the topic without
reading the answer. Recommended lab: Use Ubuntu Server in VirtualBox, VMware, WSL2, or a cloud VM. Never practise
destructive commands on a production machine. Completion Rules
☐Read the concept and explain it in your own words.
☐Type every command manually.
☐Predict the output before running commands.
☐Complete the lab and troubleshooting task.
☐Answer at least 80% of the checkpoint questions.
☐Mark the unit Completed and record the date. Volume Outcomes
After completing this volume you should be able to operate a Linux server, manage users and permissions,
control processes and services, inspect logs, troubleshoot network and storage issues, use SSH safely, and
explain how Linux is used in a DevOps team. Master Progress Dashboard

Unit 1 - Linux and DevOps Foundations
Learning objectives
☐Explain the role of Linux in DevOps
☐Describe the kernel, shell and user space
☐Identify common Linux distributions
What is Linux?
Linux is an operating-system kernel. A complete Linux operating system combines the Linux kernel with
system tools, libraries, package managers and applications. Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat Enterprise Linux,
Rocky Linux and Amazon Linux are distributions built around the kernel. Most servers, containers, CI runners, Kubernetes nodes and cloud virtual machines use Linux because it is
stable, automatable, scriptable and widely supported. Kernel, shell and commands
The kernel manages CPU, memory, disks, devices, networking and processes. The shell accepts commands
and starts programs. Bash is a common shell used in DevOps. Commands such as ls, cp and systemctl are
programs executed by the shell.
echo $SHELL
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
Linux architecture
A simplified path is: user -> terminal -> shell -> system calls -> kernel -> hardware. Applications usually do
not access hardware directly; they ask the kernel for resources. Distributions and package families
Debian-family systems commonly use apt and .deb packages. Red Hat-family systems use dnf/yum
and .rpm packages. Commands and paths are largely similar, but package names and security tools can
differ. How companies use this
DevOps teams standardise server images, package versions and configuration so environments remain
predictable. Linux is commonly the base operating system for web servers, databases, CI agents and
Kubernetes worker nodes. Hands-on lab
1. Open a terminal.
2. Run uname -a and identify the kernel version.
3. Run cat /etc/os-release and identify the distribution.

4. Run echo $SHELL and identify your shell.
5. Write a five-line explanation of why Linux is central to DevOps. Checkpoint
☐I can explain kernel versus shell.
☐I can name three Linux distributions.
☐I can explain why cloud servers commonly use Linux. Interview questions
Q: Is Linux an operating system or a kernel?
A: Technically Linux is the kernel; distributions combine it with user-space tools to form a complete
operating system. Q: Why is Linux popular in DevOps?
A: It is stable, automatable, secure, cloud-friendly and supported by most infrastructure tools. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 2 - Lab Setup and Terminal Basics
Learning objectives
☐Create a safe Linux learning environment
☐Use terminal shortcuts and command history
☐Get help for unfamiliar commands
Choosing a lab
Suitable options are an Ubuntu virtual machine, WSL2 on Windows, a spare machine, or a low-cost cloud
VM. A virtual machine is ideal because snapshots let you recover from mistakes. Prompt and command structure
A command normally has a command name, options and arguments. In ls -lah /var/log, ls is the command,
-lah contains options and /var/log is the argument. Linux is case-sensitive.
ls -lah /var/log
pwd
whoami
Help systems
Use man for manuals, --help for quick usage, and apropos to find commands by topic.
man ls
ls --help
apropos network
History and shortcuts
Use history to review commands. Ctrl+C interrupts a foreground command. Ctrl+L clears the screen. Tab
completes paths and commands. Up Arrow recalls previous commands.
history
!!
!25
Hands-on lab
1. Create or start your Linux lab.
2. Take a VM snapshot named clean-linux-lab.
3. Run pwd, whoami, hostname and date.
4. Open man ls, search for reverse sorting using /reverse, then quit with q.
5. Use Tab completion to enter /var/log. Checkpoint
☐I can distinguish command, option and argument.

☐I can use man and --help.
☐I know what Ctrl+C, Ctrl+L and Tab do. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 3 - Filesystem and Navigation
Learning objectives
☐Understand Linux directory structure
☐Navigate using absolute and relative paths
☐Inspect files and directories safely
Filesystem hierarchy
The filesystem begins at /. Important paths include /home for user data, /etc for configuration, /var for
changing data and logs, /usr for applications and libraries, /tmp for temporary files, /opt for optional
software, /srv for service data and /root for the root user. Absolute and relative paths
An absolute path begins with /. A relative path begins from the current directory. The symbols . and .. mean
current directory and parent directory. The tilde ~ refers to the current user home directory.
cd /var/log
cd ..
cd ~
pwd
Listing content
ls lists directory entries. -l shows details, -a includes hidden entries, -h makes sizes readable, and -t sorts by
modification time.
ls -lah
ls -lt /var/log
Hands-on lab
1. Create ~/devops-lab/unit3.
2. Inside it create directories app, logs and backup.
3. Navigate using both absolute and relative paths.
4. Create a hidden file named .env.
5. Run ls -lah and explain every column in the output. Checkpoint
☐I know what /, ~, . and .. mean.
☐I can identify /etc, /var/log and /home.
☐I can use absolute and relative paths. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 4 - Files, Directories, Text and Search
Learning objectives
☐Create, copy, move and remove files
☐Read and search text files
☐Use pipes and redirection
File operations
touch creates an empty file or updates timestamps. mkdir creates directories. cp copies, mv moves or
renames, and rm removes. rm -rf is destructive and must be used with extreme care.
touch app.log
mkdir -p project/{config,logs,backup}
cp app.log backup/
mv app.log application.log
Reading files
cat is suitable for short files. less is better for large files. head and tail show the beginning or end. tail -f
follows appended log lines in real time.
cat /etc/hostname
less /var/log/syslog
head -n 10 file.txt
tail -f app.log
Searching
grep searches text. find searches paths and metadata. Use grep -i for case-insensitive matching, -r for
recursive search and -n for line numbers.
grep -in "error" app.log
find /var/log -type f -name "*.log" 2>/dev/null
Pipes and redirection
A pipe sends one command output into another command. > overwrites a file, >> appends, and 2> redirects
errors.
ps aux | grep nginx
echo "start" > app.log
echo "next" >> app.log
find /root 2> errors.txt
Hands-on lab
1. Create a ten-line log file containing INFO, WARNING and ERROR messages.
2. Use grep to show only ERROR lines with line numbers.
3. Use tail to show the final three lines.
4. Redirect the result into errors-only.log.

5. Use find to locate every .log file inside your lab. Checkpoint
☐I understand > versus >>.
☐I can explain a pipe.
☐I can use grep and find for troubleshooting. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 5 - Users, Groups and Identity
Learning objectives
☐Inspect users and groups
☐Create and manage accounts
☐Understand UID, GID and login identity
Identity model
Each user has a UID and primary GID. Groups allow shared access. Account information is stored in
/etc/passwd; password hashes are protected in /etc/shadow; group information is stored in /etc/group.
id
whoami
groups
getent passwd $USER
User management
Administrative commands include useradd or adduser, passwd, usermod and userdel. On Ubuntu, adduser
provides an interactive workflow.
sudo adduser devopsstudent
sudo usermod -aG sudo devopsstudent
sudo passwd devopsstudent
Switching identity
su starts a shell as another user. sudo runs a command with delegated privileges. sudo -i starts a root login
shell when permitted.
su - devopsstudent
sudo whoami
sudo -i
Hands-on lab
1. Create a user named labuser.
2. Create a group named devteam.
3. Add labuser to devteam without removing existing group membership.
4. Verify membership with id labuser.
5. Lock and unlock the account, then remove it after the lab. Checkpoint
☐I can explain UID and GID.
☐I know why usermod -aG includes -a.

☐I understand su versus sudo. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 6 - Permissions, Ownership and sudo
Learning objectives
☐Read symbolic and numeric permissions
☐Change mode and ownership
☐Apply least privilege
Permission structure
Permissions are read, write and execute for owner, group and others. For files, execute means runnable. For directories, execute means traversal. Numeric values are read=4, write=2 and execute=1.
ls -l
chmod 750 deploy.sh
chmod u+x deploy.sh
Ownership
chown changes owner and optionally group. chgrp changes group. Recursive changes should be reviewed
carefully.
sudo chown appuser:devteam application.conf
sudo chgrp devteam application.conf
Special permissions
setuid, setgid and sticky bit are special modes. The sticky bit on shared directories such as /tmp prevents
users from deleting files owned by others.
ls -ld /tmp
chmod 1777 shared-dir
sudo policy
sudo permissions are configured in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d. Always edit using visudo to validate
syntax. Grant only commands required for the role.
sudo visudo
Hands-on lab
1. Create deploy.sh and set permission 750.
2. Create a shared directory owned by group devteam with mode 2770.
3. Explain why 777 is usually unsafe.
4. Use stat to inspect file ownership and numeric mode.
5. Create a safe sudoers example that permits restarting nginx only.

Checkpoint
☐I can translate rwxr-x--- into 750.
☐I understand directory execute permission.
☐I can explain least privilege. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 7 - Processes and Job Control
Learning objectives
☐Inspect running processes
☐Send signals safely
☐Manage foreground and background jobs
Processes
Every running program has a PID. ps provides snapshots. top and htop provide interactive monitoring. Important metrics include CPU, memory, state, user and elapsed time.
ps aux
ps -ef
top
Signals
kill sends a signal to a PID. SIGTERM asks a process to exit gracefully. SIGKILL forces termination and
should be a last resort. killall and pkill target names or patterns.
kill 2451
kill -15 2451
kill -9 2451
pkill -f "python app.py"
Jobs
Appending & starts a command in the background. jobs lists shell jobs. fg and bg move jobs between
foreground and background. nohup helps a process continue after logout, although managed services are
preferred in production.
sleep 300 &
jobs
fg %1
nohup ./app.sh > app.out 2>&1 &
Hands-on lab
1. Start sleep 300 in the background.
2. Find its PID using ps or pgrep.
3. Send SIGTERM and confirm it exits.
4. Start another sleep process and practise Ctrl+Z, bg and fg.
5. Explain when SIGKILL is justified. Checkpoint
☐I can find a PID.

☐I know SIGTERM versus SIGKILL.
☐I can manage jobs. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 8 - systemd and Service Management
Learning objectives
☐Understand units and service lifecycle
☐Start, stop, restart and enable services
☐Create a basic custom service
systemd
systemd is the init and service manager on many modern Linux distributions. Units describe services,
timers, mounts, sockets and other resources. Core commands
start changes the current state; enable configures startup at boot. reload asks a service to reread
configuration when supported. status shows state and recent logs.
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl reload nginx
systemctl status nginx
Custom unit
A service file normally belongs in /etc/systemd/system. After editing units, run daemon-reload.
[Unit]
Description=Demo Application
After=network.target
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/demo-app
Restart=on-failure
User=demo
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
Hands-on lab
1. Install nginx in your lab.
2. Start it and confirm active status.
3. Enable it and verify is-enabled.
4. Stop it, test the endpoint, then start it again.
5. Create a harmless custom oneshot service that writes the date to /tmp/service-test.txt.

Checkpoint
☐I understand start versus enable.
☐I can use status and is-enabled.
☐I know why daemon-reload is required. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 9 - Logs and Debugging
Learning objectives
☐Locate system and application logs
☐Use journalctl effectively
☐Follow a structured debugging process
Log sources
Traditional logs often live under /var/log. systemd collects journal events accessed through journalctl. Applications may log to files, stdout/stderr, syslog or a central platform.
ls -lah /var/log
journalctl -n 50
Service logs
Filter by unit, time, priority or boot. Use -f to follow.
journalctl -u nginx
journalctl -u nginx -f
journalctl --since "30 minutes ago"
journalctl -p err -b
Debugging method
Use the sequence: define symptom, reproduce, check service state, inspect logs, confirm configuration,
confirm dependencies, test locally, test network path, change one thing, verify and document. Log filtering
Combine grep, awk, sort and uniq to summarise repeated events.
grep -i "error" app.log
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
Hands-on lab
1. Break the nginx configuration deliberately with a safe typo after making a backup.
2. Run nginx -t and record the error.
3. Restart nginx and inspect systemctl status plus journalctl -u nginx.
4. Restore the configuration and verify recovery.
5. Write a mini incident note containing symptom, cause, fix and prevention. Checkpoint
☐I can use journalctl -u and -f.
☐I check logs before guessing.

☐I can describe a repeatable troubleshooting method. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 10 - Networking Fundamentals
Learning objectives
☐Understand IP, ports, protocols and DNS
☐Inspect interfaces, routes and listening services
☐Troubleshoot connectivity layer by layer
Core concepts
An IP address identifies a network interface. A port identifies an application endpoint. TCP is connection-
oriented; UDP is connectionless. DNS translates names to addresses. Common ports include 22 SSH, 53 DNS,
80 HTTP and 443 HTTPS. Interface and route commands
ip replaces older ifconfig and route commands on modern systems.
ip address
ip link
ip route
Connectivity tests
ping tests ICMP reachability when allowed. curl tests application endpoints. ss shows sockets. dig or
nslookup tests DNS. traceroute shows the network path.
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
curl -I http://localhost
ss -tulnp
dig example.com
traceroute example.com
Troubleshooting order
Check local process, listening port, local curl, firewall, interface, route, DNS, remote reachability, load
balancer and application logs. A successful ping does not prove the application is healthy. Hands-on lab
1. Run ip a and identify your active interface.
2. Run ip route and identify the default gateway.
3. Start nginx and confirm port 80 with ss -tulnp.
4. Run curl -I localhost and interpret the HTTP status.
5. Use dig to resolve a domain and identify the returned IP address. Checkpoint
☐I can explain IP versus port.

☐I can use ss and curl.
☐I can separate DNS, transport and application failures. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 11 - Packages and Software Management
Learning objectives
☐Use apt and dnf/yum safely
☐Understand repositories and package metadata
☐Verify installed software
Package managers
Package managers resolve dependencies, verify packages and track installed files. Ubuntu/Debian
commonly use apt; RHEL-family systems use dnf.
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nginx
apt list --installed
sudo apt remove nginx
Red Hat family
Equivalent commands use dnf.
sudo dnf check-update
sudo dnf install nginx
dnf list installed
Operational safety
In companies, package changes are tested, reviewed and automated. Avoid unplanned upgrades on
production servers. Record versions and maintain rollback plans.
nginx -v
dpkg -l | grep nginx
rpm -qa | grep nginx
Hands-on lab
1. Install tree and jq.
2. Verify their versions.
3. Identify which package owns a binary.
4. Remove one package and verify removal.
5. Explain apt update versus apt upgrade. Checkpoint
☐I can install and remove packages.
☐I understand repository metadata.
☐I avoid uncontrolled production upgrades.

Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 12 - Storage, Disks and Filesystems
Learning objectives
☐Inspect disks and filesystem usage
☐Find large files and directories
☐Understand mounts, inodes and LVM basics
Disk views
lsblk shows block devices. df reports filesystem usage. du measures directory/file usage. A filesystem can
run out of blocks or inodes.
lsblk -f
df -h
df -i
du -xhd1 /var | sort -h
Mounting
A filesystem is attached to the directory tree at a mount point. /etc/fstab describes persistent mounts. Incorrect fstab entries can affect boot, so test with mount -a.
findmnt
cat /etc/fstab
sudo mount -a
LVM overview
Logical Volume Manager separates physical storage from logical volumes. It supports flexible resizing and
snapshots, but operations must be planned and backed up.
sudo pvs
sudo vgs
sudo lvs
Hands-on lab
1. Run lsblk -f and map devices to mount points.
2. Run df -h and identify the fullest filesystem.
3. Use du to find the largest directory inside your lab.
4. Create many small files and observe inode usage with df -i.
5. Explain why deleting an open log may not immediately free space. Checkpoint
☐I know df versus du.
☐I can investigate a full disk.

☐I understand block usage versus inode usage. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 13 - SSH and Remote Administration
Learning objectives
☐Connect securely to remote Linux systems
☐Use key-based authentication
☐Transfer files and troubleshoot SSH
SSH basics
SSH provides encrypted remote login and command execution. The client connects to sshd, usually on TCP
port 22.
ssh user@server-ip
ssh -p 2222 user@server-ip
Keys
A key pair includes a private key kept secret and a public key installed on the server. Protect private keys
with correct permissions and preferably a passphrase.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id user@server-ip
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
Transfers
scp copies files. rsync efficiently synchronises content and can preserve attributes.
scp app.tar.gz user@server:/tmp/
rsync -avz project/ user@server:/srv/project/
Troubleshooting
Use ssh -v for verbose diagnostics. Check network reachability, port 22, sshd status, firewall, user account,
key permissions and server logs.
ssh -v user@server
sudo systemctl status ssh
sudo journalctl -u ssh
Hands-on lab
1. Create an SSH key pair in your lab.
2. Inspect public and private key permissions.
3. Connect to a second VM or localhost SSH server using a key.
4. Transfer a test file using scp.
5. Use ssh -v and identify authentication stages.

Checkpoint
☐I understand public versus private keys.
☐I can use scp and rsync.
☐I can troubleshoot SSH authentication. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 14 - Security and Hardening Basics
Learning objectives
☐Apply least privilege and secure defaults
☐Use firewall and update practices
☐Recognise common Linux security controls
Security principles
Use least privilege, defence in depth, secure configuration, timely patching, strong authentication, logging
and tested backups. Disable unused services and ports. Firewall
Ubuntu commonly uses ufw as a front end. RHEL commonly uses firewalld. Always preserve SSH access
before enabling remote firewall rules.
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose
SSH hardening
Prefer keys, restrict root login, remove unused accounts and review authentication logs. Test configuration
before reloading sshd.
sudo sshd -t
sudo journalctl -u ssh --since today
Mandatory access control
SELinux and AppArmor apply policy beyond standard Unix permissions. Do not disable them as a first
troubleshooting step; inspect denials and correct policy or context.
getenforce
sestatus
sudo aa-status
Hands-on lab
1. List listening ports and identify unnecessary services.
2. Enable a firewall in the lab while preserving SSH access.
3. Review failed login events.
4. Check for available security updates.
5. Write a ten-point Linux hardening checklist.

Checkpoint
☐I understand least privilege.
☐I can describe firewall purpose.
☐I know why disabling SELinux/AppArmor is poor practice. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 15 - Performance and Resource Troubleshooting
Learning objectives
☐Interpret CPU, memory, load and I/O signals
☐Find resource-heavy processes
☐Use a structured performance workflow
CPU and load
Load average represents runnable or uninterruptible work over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare load with
CPU count. High load may come from CPU or I/O waits.
uptime
nproc
top
Memory
free shows memory totals and available memory. Linux uses free memory for cache; low free memory
alone is not necessarily a problem. Watch available memory, swap and OOM events.
free -h
vmstat 1
journalctl -k | grep -i oom
I/O and files
iostat, pidstat and lsof help investigate disks and open files. These may require sysstat or lsof packages.
iostat -xz 1
pidstat 1
lsof +L1
Workflow
Measure before changing. Identify the constrained resource, isolate the process, correlate with logs and
deployments, reduce impact, fix root cause and monitor after recovery. Hands-on lab
1. Record uptime, CPU count and load average.
2. Identify the top three CPU and memory processes.
3. Run a temporary CPU load in the lab and observe top.
4. Inspect swap usage.
5. Use lsof +L1 to check for deleted-but-open files. Checkpoint
☐I can explain load average.

☐I understand available memory.
☐I measure before tuning. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 16 - Scheduling with cron and at
Learning objectives
☐Schedule recurring and one-time jobs
☐Manage cron environment and logs
☐Prevent duplicate or unsafe jobs
Cron syntax
Cron fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. Commands run with a limited
environment, so use absolute paths and redirect output.
crontab -e
# m h dom mon dow command
0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1
One-time jobs
at schedules a one-time command when the at service is available.
echo "/usr/local/bin/report.sh" | at 18:00
Reliability
Scripts should use locking, clear exit codes, logging and alerting. systemd timers are often preferred for
richer control and observability. Hands-on lab
1. Create a script that appends date to /tmp/cron-test.log.
2. Schedule it every minute temporarily.
3. Verify execution and locate cron logs.
4. Remove the test schedule.
5. Explain how you would prevent overlapping backup jobs. Checkpoint
☐I can read cron fields.
☐I use absolute paths.
☐I know cron has a limited environment. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 17 - Archives, Compression and Transfers
Learning objectives
☐Create and extract archives
☐Choose common compression formats
☐Verify backups and transfers
tar and compression
tar groups files into an archive. gzip and xz compress data. Common extensions include .tar.gz and .tar.xz.
tar -czf project.tar.gz project/
tar -tzf project.tar.gz
tar -xzf project.tar.gz
Integrity
A backup is not complete until restoration is tested. Checksums detect corruption or transfer changes.
sha256sum project.tar.gz
sha256sum -c project.tar.gz.sha256
Transfers
Use rsync for repeatable synchronisation and scp for simple copies. In production, define encryption,
retention and restore tests. Hands-on lab
1. Archive your lab directory.
2. List archive contents without extraction.
3. Create a SHA-256 checksum.
4. Extract into a new directory and compare files.
5. Document a backup retention and restore-test plan. Checkpoint
☐I can create and extract tar.gz.
☐I can verify checksums.
☐I understand that backup success requires restore testing. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint
without notes.

Unit 18 - Company Workflow and Incident Handling
Learning objectives
☐Understand daily DevOps Linux work
☐Follow change and incident processes
☐Write operational documentation
Daily workflow
A DevOps engineer may review alerts, investigate incidents, support deployments, manage configuration,
improve automation, patch systems, review capacity and document changes. Work is usually tracked in
tickets and repositories. Change management
A production change should have scope, owner, risk, test evidence, rollout steps, rollback steps, monitoring
and approval. Emergency changes still require documentation after stabilisation. Incident lifecycle
Detect, acknowledge, assess severity, stabilise service, communicate, investigate, recover, verify, document
timeline, perform root-cause analysis and track corrective actions. Avoid blame; focus on system
improvements. Runbooks and postmortems
A runbook describes repeatable operational actions. A postmortem documents impact, timeline, root cause,
contributing factors, resolution and prevention. Hands-on lab
1. Write a change plan to upgrade nginx in production.
2. Include validation and rollback steps.
3. Simulate an nginx outage and write an incident timeline.
4. Create a one-page nginx recovery runbook.
5. Write three preventive actions after the incident. Checkpoint
☐I can distinguish incident, problem and change.
☐I can write rollback steps.
☐I understand blameless postmortems. Completion gate: Mark this unit Completed only after the lab works and you can answer the checkpoint

Interview Question Bank
Q: What happens after you type a command in Bash?
A: Bash parses the command, performs expansions and redirections, locates the executable or built-in,
starts it, and the program uses system calls to request kernel services. Q: What is the difference between a process and a service?
A: A process is a running program. A service is a long-running function normally managed by a service
manager such as systemd and may include restart and boot policies. Q: What is the difference between hard and symbolic links?
A: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode and normally cannot cross filesystems. A
symbolic link stores a path and can cross filesystems but can become broken. Q: Why can df and du show different values?
A: Deleted but still-open files, filesystem metadata, reserved blocks, mount boundaries and sparse files can
cause differences. Q: What does chmod 750 mean?
A: Owner has rwx, group has r-x, and others have no permissions. Q: How do you investigate a full disk?
A: Use df -h and df -i, identify the filesystem, use du within the same filesystem, inspect logs and deleted-
open files with lsof +L1, then remediate safely. Q: How do you investigate an inaccessible web application?
A: Check process/service, logs, listening port, local curl, configuration, dependencies, firewall,
route/DNS/load balancer and remote curl. Q: Why use SIGTERM before SIGKILL?
A: SIGTERM allows graceful cleanup; SIGKILL cannot be handled and may cause data loss or inconsistent
state. Q: What is load average?
A: The average number of runnable and uninterruptible tasks over 1, 5 and 15 minutes; interpret it
relative to CPU count and I/O behaviour. Q: What is the difference between systemctl start and enable?

A: start changes the current running state; enable configures the unit to start automatically according to
boot targets. Q: How do you find which process owns a port?
A: Use ss -ltnp or ss -tulnp, optionally filtering the port. Q: What is an inode?
A: Filesystem metadata object representing a file, excluding its filename; it stores ownership, mode,
timestamps and block pointers. Q: How does sudo differ from su?
A: sudo runs authorised commands under another identity using policy and auditing; su switches to
another user shell and commonly requires that account password or root access. Q: What should a production change include?
A: Scope, risk, owner, test evidence, implementation, validation, monitoring, rollback and communication. Q: Why should logs be centralised?
A: Centralisation supports searching across hosts, retention, access control, alerting and investigation even
if a server is lost. Scenario Questions
